claim: Kinesin-1 and cytoplasmic dynein are microtubule (MT) motors that transport intracellular cargoes.
source: Kinesin-1 and cytoplasmic dynein are microtubule (MT) motors that transport intracellular cargoes.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology supported by extensive prior research and is stated as background knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Single mammalian dynein is highly capable of bypassing obstacles.
source: Contrary to previous reports, we found that single mammalian dynein is highly capable of bypassing obstacles.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 where DDB motors maintain high mobile fraction, velocity, and run length even at high QD obstacle densities.

claim: Single human kinesin-1 motors fail to avoid obstacles.
source: Single human kinesin-1 motors fail to avoid obstacles, consistent with their inability to take sideways steps on to neighboring MT protofilaments.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1 showing dramatic reduction in mobile fraction, velocity, and run length of kinesin in the presence of obstacles, and is consistent with prior knowledge about kinesin stepping behavior.

claim: Single human kinesin-1 motors are unable to take sideways steps on to neighboring MT protofilaments.
source: Single human kinesin-1 motors fail to avoid obstacles, consistent with their inability to take sideways steps on to neighboring MT protofilaments.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript and is consistent with the experimental observations.

claim: Kinesins overcome their limitation in bypassing obstacles when working in teams.
source: Kinesins overcome this limitation when working in teams, bypassing obstacles as effectively as multiple dyneins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing that beads coated with multiple kinesins maintain high mobile fraction even at high obstacle densities.

claim: Cargos driven by multiple kinesins or dyneins are capable of rotating around the MT to bypass large obstacles.
source: Cargos driven by multiple kinesins or dyneins are also capable of rotating around the MT to bypass large obstacles.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing beads rotating around MT bridges when encountering PDMS walls.

claim: Multiplicity of motors is required for maneuvering cargos on obstacle-coated MT surfaces.
source: These results suggest that multiplicity of motors is required not only for transporting cargos over long distances and generating higher forces, but also for maneuvering cargos on obstacle-coated MT surfaces.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that multiple motors bypass obstacles more effectively than single motors.

claim: Kinesin and dynein have complementary functions on MTs.
source: Although these motors have complementary functions on MTs, they have distinct structural and mechanistic features.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge that kinesin moves toward plus-ends and dynein toward minus-ends of MTs.

claim: Kinesin-1 contains a globular motor domain that binds the MT and hydrolyzes ATP.
source: Kinesin-1 contains a globular motor domain that binds the MT and hydrolyzes ATP.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about kinesin-1 supported by citation.

claim: Two identical motor domains of kinesin are connected by a short neck-linker to a common tail.
source: Two identical motor domains are connected by a short neck-linker to a common tail (Figure 1A) (Verhey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Kinesin moves by coordinated stepping of its motor domains, in a manner akin to human walking.
source: In vitro studies have shown that kinesin moves by coordinated stepping of its motor domains, in a manner akin to human walking (Yildiz et al., 2004; Asbury et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by prior in vitro studies as indicated by the citations.

claim: Kinesin follows a single protofilament track on the MT.
source: It follows a single protofilament track on the MT and almost exclusively steps forward without frequent sideways or backward motion (Ray et al., 1993; Can et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citations.

claim: Kinesin almost exclusively steps forward without frequent sideways or backward motion.
source: It follows a single protofilament track on the MT and almost exclusively steps forward without frequent sideways or backward motion (Ray et al., 1993; Can et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citations.

claim: Dynein's motor domains are large heterohexameric rings of AAA+ ATPase subunits that connect to the MT through a coiled-coil stalk.
source: Unlike kinesin, dynein's motor domains are large heterohexameric rings of AAA+ ATPase subunits that connect to the MT through a coiled-coil stalk (Figure 1A) (Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Stepping of the dynein motor domains is not tightly coordinated.
source: Stepping of the dynein motor domains is not tightly coordinated (DeWitt et al., 2012; Qiu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citations.

claim: Either dynein monomer can take a step while the other serves as an MT tether.
source: Instead, either monomer can take a step while the other serves as an MT tether (DeWitt et al., 2012; Reck-Peterson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citations.

claim: Dynein has a large diffusional component in its stepping behavior, resulting in frequent sideways and backward steps.
source: Dynein has a large diffusional component in its stepping behavior, resulting in frequent sideways and backward steps (DeWitt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: Differences in the stepping behaviors between kinesin and dynein may influence their cellular functions.
source: Differences in the stepping behaviors between these motors may influence their cellular functions (Hancock, 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation and logical inference from the different stepping mechanisms.

claim: Intracellular transport takes place in a highly crowded and dynamic cytoplasm.
source: Intracellular transport takes place in a highly crowded and dynamic cytoplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the cellular environment.

claim: The MT network is densely decorated with obstacles such as MT-associated proteins (MAPs), stationary organelles, protein aggregates, MT defects, opposing motor traffic and other cytoskeletal filaments.
source: The MT network is densely decorated with obstacles such as MT-associated proteins (MAPs), stationary organelles, protein aggregates, MT defects, opposing motor traffic and other cytoskeletal filaments (Dixit et al., 2008; Che et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citations.

claim: Motors need to take sideways steps to avoid obstacles on their path.
source: Previous in vitro studies suggested that motors need to take sideways steps to avoid obstacles on their path (Schneider et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: Kinesin motility is strongly inhibited by obstacles such as catalytically-inactive motors, MAPs or cell extract.
source: In agreement with this idea, kinesin motility is strongly inhibited by obstacles such as catalytically-inactive motors, MAPs or cell extract (Schneider et al., 2015; Dixit et al., 2008; Telley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citations.

claim: Kinesin motors can occasionally bypass obstacles by detaching and reattaching to neighboring protofilaments.
source: While these motors can occasionally bypass obstacles by detaching and reattaching to neighboring protofilaments, they stall or detach from the MT in most cases (Schneider et al., 2015; Leduc et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citations.

claim: Kinesin motors stall or detach from the MT in most cases when encountering obstacles.
source: While these motors can occasionally bypass obstacles by detaching and reattaching to neighboring protofilaments, they stall or detach from the MT in most cases (Schneider et al., 2015; Leduc et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citations.

claim: Kinesin-2 has faster MT detachment/reattachment kinetics than kinesin-1.
source: Kinesin-2, a different kinesin family member with faster MT detachment/reattachment kinetics (Feng et al., 2018) and increased side-stepping ability (Hoeprich et al., 2014), bypasses obstacles more successfully than kinesin-1.
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: Kinesin-2 has increased side-stepping ability compared to kinesin-1.
source: Kinesin-2, a different kinesin family member with faster MT detachment/reattachment kinetics (Feng et al., 2018) and increased side-stepping ability (Hoeprich et al., 2014), bypasses obstacles more successfully than kinesin-1.
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: Kinesin-2 bypasses obstacles more successfully than kinesin-1.
source: Kinesin-2, a different kinesin family member with faster MT detachment/reattachment kinetics (Feng et al., 2018) and increased side-stepping ability (Hoeprich et al., 2014), bypasses obstacles more successfully than kinesin-1.
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citations and logical inference from the properties of kinesin-2.

claim: Dynein was expected to be less sensitive to obstacles than kinesin because of its elongated structure and frequent sideways stepping.
source: Dynein was expected to be less sensitive to obstacles than kinesin because of its elongated structure and frequent sideways stepping (DeWitt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior knowledge about dynein structure and stepping behavior.

claim: In vitro studies on isolated mammalian dynein observed that the motor reverses direction when encountering a MAP obstacle rather than bypassing it.
source: Yet, in vitro studies on isolated mammalian dynein observed that the motor reverses direction when encountering a MAP obstacle rather than bypassing it (Dixit et al., 2008; Soundararajan and Bullock, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citations.

claim: Mammalian dynein alone is autoinhibited and its activation requires assembly with dynactin and a cargo adaptor.
source: However, these studies were conducted before it was understood that mammalian dynein alone is autoinhibited and its activation requires assembly with dynactin and a cargo adaptor (Schlager et al., 2014; McKenney et al., 2014; Trokter et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by prior research as indicated by the citations.

claim: Cytoskeletal motors often operate in teams to transport a cargo.
source: Unlike helicases, unfoldases and DNA/RNA polymerases, which usually function as individual motors (Singleton et al., 2007), cytoskeletal motors often operate in teams to transport a cargo (Encalada et al., 2011; Rai et al., 2016; Levi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citations.

claim: Multiple motors carry cargos with increased processivity relative to single motors.
source: Multiple motors carry cargos with increased processivity relative to single motors (Derr et al., 2012), which is essential for long-range transport in cell types such as neurons.
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: Teams of motors exert higher forces, which may enable the transport of large cargos through the dense cellular environment.
source: Teams of motors also exert higher forces, which may enable the transport of large cargos through the dense cellular environment (Blehm et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation and involves speculation about the functional consequence.

claim: Cargos with multiple motors avoid obstacles more effectively than single motors.
source: It has been proposed that cargos with multiple motors also avoid obstacles more effectively than single motors (Hancock, 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: Multi-kinesin cargos pause at MT defects rather than detach like single motors.
source: A recent study found that multi-kinesin cargos pause at MT defects rather than detach like single motors (Liang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: Ensembles of two kinesin-1 motors linked together with a DNA scaffold have a higher run length than single kinesins.
source: Ensembles of two kinesin-1 motors linked together with a DNA scaffold have a higher run length than single kinesins, but their run length was also decreased in the presence of neutravidin obstacles on the MT (Feng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: The run length of ensembles of two kinesin-1 motors was decreased in the presence of neutravidin obstacles on the MT.
source: Ensembles of two kinesin-1 motors linked together with a DNA scaffold have a higher run length than single kinesins, but their run length was also decreased in the presence of neutravidin obstacles on the MT (Feng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: Single dynein motors efficiently navigate around obstacles.
source: We find that kinesin and dynein employ different mechanisms to bypass these obstacles. Consistent with their ability to take side-steps, single dynein motors efficiently navigate around obstacles.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1 showing that dynein maintains high motility parameters even at high obstacle densities.

claim: Single kinesins are strongly inhibited by QDs and antibodies on MTs.
source: Unlike dynein, single kinesins are strongly inhibited by QDs and antibodies on MTs yet overcome this limitation when working together as a team.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 3 showing dramatic reduction in kinesin motility parameters in the presence of obstacles.

claim: Single kinesins overcome their limitation when working together as a team.
source: Unlike dynein, single kinesins are strongly inhibited by QDs and antibodies on MTs yet overcome this limitation when working together as a team.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing that multiple kinesins on beads maintain high motility even at high obstacle densities.

claim: The multiplicity of motors is critical to bypass large roadblocks.
source: The multiplicity of motors was also critical to bypass large roadblocks.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing that multi-motor cargos can rotate around MTs to bypass PDMS walls.

claim: When cargos driven by a team of kinesin or dynein motors face a wall along their path, they swing around the MT without net forward movement and continue moving forward.
source: When cargos driven by a team of kinesin or dynein motors face a wall along their path, they swing around the MT without net forward movement and continue moving forward.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing rotation of beads around MTs when encountering PDMS walls.

claim: QDs have a bright and photostable fluorescent emission.
source: These QDs have a bright and photostable fluorescent emission, which enable us to measure their linear density along MTs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the properties of quantum dots.

claim: Human kinesin-1 was truncated at its coiled-coil stalk (expressing amino acids 1–560) and fused to GFP and HaloTag at its C-terminus.
source: Human kinesin-1 was truncated at its coiled-coil stalk (expressing amino acids 1–560) and fused to GFP and HaloTag at its C-terminus (Belyy et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the experimental construct used in the study, supported by citation.

claim: The N-terminal tail domain of yeast cytoplasmic dynein was replaced with a glutathione S-transferase (GST) tag for dimerization and a HaloTag for labeling.
source: The N-terminal tail domain of yeast cytoplasmic dynein was replaced with a glutathione S-transferase (GST) tag for dimerization and a HaloTag for labeling (GST–Dyn331kD, expressing amino acids 1219–4093 of the dynein heavy chain) (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes the experimental construct used in the study, supported by citation.

claim: The DDB complex was assembled using full-length human cytoplasmic dynein, pig brain dynactin and N-terminal coiled-coil of mouse BicD2 (BicD2N).
source: The DDB complex was assembled using full-length human cytoplasmic dynein, pig brain dynactin and N-terminal coiled-coil of mouse BicD2 (BicD2N).
evidence: This describes the experimental complex used in the study.

claim: A human dynein mutant that does not form the autoinhibited conformation was used to facilitate DDB assembly.
source: To facilitate DDB assembly, we used a human dynein mutant that does not form the autoinhibited conformation (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study, supported by citation.

claim: The run lengths of kinesin-QD complexes (2.1 ± 0.2 µm, mean ± SD) were similar to kinesin motors labeled with an organic dye.
source: The run lengths of kinesin-QD complexes (2.1 ± 0.2 µm, mean ± SD) were similar to kinesin motors labeled with an organic dye (p=0.21, two-tailed t-test, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E), suggesting that QDs were driven by single motors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing QD-labeled and dye-labeled kinesin.

claim: QDs were driven by single motors.
source: The run lengths of kinesin-QD complexes (2.1 ± 0.2 µm, mean ± SD) were similar to kinesin motors labeled with an organic dye (p=0.21, two-tailed t-test, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E), suggesting that QDs were driven by single motors.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity in run lengths between QD-labeled and dye-labeled kinesin.

claim: Single yeast dynein and DDB motors walked processively even at the highest QD density tested.
source: Consistent with dynein's ability to take side-steps, we found that single yeast dynein and DDB motors walked processively even at the highest QD density tested (Figure 1D,E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Video 1) (DeWitt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: Previously observed reversals of mammalian dynein might be due to diffusive motion of this motor in the absence of dynactin and a cargo adaptor.
source: We did not see evidence of motor reversals when DDB encountered a QD obstacle, suggesting that previously observed reversals of mammalian dynein might be due to diffusive motion of this motor in the absence of dynactin and a cargo adaptor (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014; Trokter et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that DDB does not reverse, combined with prior knowledge about dynein autoinhibition.

claim: Mobile fraction, velocity and run length of yeast dynein were reduced 30–70% by increasing density of QDs.
source: While mobile fraction, velocity and run length of yeast dynein were reduced 30–70% by increasing density of QDs, DDB motility was less sensitive to obstacles.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: DDB motility was less sensitive to obstacles than yeast dynein.
source: While mobile fraction, velocity and run length of yeast dynein were reduced 30–70% by increasing density of QDs, DDB motility was less sensitive to obstacles.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E comparing yeast dynein and DDB.

claim: Kinesin motility was severely affected by the QDs.
source: In comparison to dynein motors, kinesin motility was severely affected by the QDs (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: The majority of kinesins became stuck on the MT with the addition of QDs.
source: The majority of kinesins became stuck on the MT with the addition of QDs (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: At low QD density (1–2 µm−1), the mobile fraction of kinesin was reduced 90%.
source: At low QD density (1–2 µm−1), the mobile fraction was reduced 90%, while the run length and velocity were reduced by 60% compared to the 0 QDs µm−1 (p=0.0003, Figure 1E, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At low QD density (1–2 µm−1), the run length and velocity of kinesin were reduced by 60%.
source: At low QD density (1–2 µm−1), the mobile fraction was reduced 90%, while the run length and velocity were reduced by 60% compared to the 0 QDs µm−1 (p=0.0003, Figure 1E, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Kinesin remains bound to an MT but is unable to move forward when it encounters a QD obstacle.
source: Collectively, these results show that kinesin remains bound to an MT but is unable to move forward when it encounters a QD obstacle.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations showing kinesin getting stuck on MTs with QD obstacles.

claim: Kinesin pause density increased two-fold at 2 QDs µm−1.
source: Strikingly, kinesin pause density increased two-fold and pause time increased four-fold at 2 QDs µm−1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Kinesin pause time increased four-fold at 2 QDs µm−1.
source: Strikingly, kinesin pause density increased two-fold and pause time increased four-fold at 2 QDs µm−1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Pause density and duration of yeast dynein and DDB were only modestly increased by the QD density.
source: In contrast, pause density and duration of yeast dynein and DDB were only modestly increased by the QD density (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Transient pauses may correspond to detachment of kinesin when encountering an obstacle and reattachment to a nearby protofilament.
source: Transient pauses may correspond to detachment of kinesin when encountering an obstacle and reattachment to a nearby protofilament (Schneider et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior research and the experimental observations.

claim: Kinesin motility stalls permanently usually after a few transient pauses in motility.
source: However, this mechanism is not robust enough to efficiently bypass obstacles, and kinesin motility stalls permanently usually after a few transient pauses in motility.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations of kinesin pausing behavior.

claim: Dynein rarely pauses permanently even at the highest density of QDs.
source: However, unlike kinesin, it rarely pauses permanently even at the highest density of QDs (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Single kinesin motors detach from MT when encountering small protein obstacles.
source: Collectively, our results show that single kinesins detach from MT when encountering small protein obstacles.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing reduced run length and mobile fraction with antibody obstacles.

claim: Kinesin motors that carry a rigid QD cargo are more likely to pause when encountering a bulkier obstacle on an MT.
source: However, kinesin motors that carry a rigid QD cargo are more likely to pause when encountering a bulkier obstacle on an MT.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the behavior of kinesin with QD obstacles versus antibody obstacles.

claim: Single kinesin motors are more strongly inhibited by antibody obstacles than DDB.
source: Similar to QD obstacles, we see that single kinesin motors are more strongly inhibited by antibody obstacles than DDB (p=0.013 for velocity and 0.01 for run length, two-tailed t-test, Figure 3B,C, Videos 3–4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Kinesin run length and velocity were reduced by ~70% at 20 µg/mL antibody.
source: Kinesin run length and velocity were reduced by ~70% at 20 µg/mL antibody (p=0.01 and 0.0001, respectively, two-tailed t-test, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was not a significant difference between the mobile fraction of kinesin and dynein at 20 µg/mL antibody.
source: In contrast to QD-obstacles, there was not a significant difference between the mobile fraction of kinesin and dynein at 20 µg/mL antibody (p=0.15, two-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing kinesin and dynein mobile fractions at 20 µg/mL antibody.

claim: Antibody obstacles inhibit kinesin by causing them to detach rather than pausing for extended periods.
source: Thus, antibody obstacles inhibit kinesin by causing them to detach rather than pausing for extended periods.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that extended pauses were not observed with antibody obstacles.

claim: Yeast dynein's run length was 2.5-fold higher on MT bridges compared to surface-immobilized MTs at 12 QD µm−1.
source: Interestingly, yeast dynein's run length was 2.5-fold higher on MT bridges compared to surface-immobilized MTs at 12 QD µm−1 (p<0.001, two-tailed t-test, Figure 1E, Figure 4C), suggesting that this motor bypasses obstacles more successfully by exploring the entire MT surface.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing yeast dynein on MT bridges versus surface-immobilized MTs.

claim: Yeast dynein bypasses obstacles more successfully by exploring the entire MT surface.
source: Interestingly, yeast dynein's run length was 2.5-fold higher on MT bridges compared to surface-immobilized MTs at 12 QD µm−1 (p<0.001, two-tailed t-test, Figure 1E, Figure 4C), suggesting that this motor bypasses obstacles more successfully by exploring the entire MT surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the improved performance on MT bridges where the entire surface is accessible.

claim: There was no significant improvement in kinesin motility on MT bridges in comparison to surface-immobilized MTs.
source: However, we did not observe a significant improvement in kinesin motility on MT bridges in comparison to surface-immobilized MTs (Figure 1E, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing kinesin on MT bridges versus surface-immobilized MTs.

claim: The mobile fraction of kinesin was reduced by 75% at 1 QD µm−1 on MT bridges compared to the no obstacle condition.
source: The mobile fraction was reduced by 75% at 1 QD µm−1 compared to the no obstacle condition, and motility could not be detected at 7 QDs µm−1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on MT bridges shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Kinesin is intrinsically limited by its ability to side-step to adjacent protofilaments when it encounters obstacles on an MT.
source: These results suggest that kinesin is intrinsically limited by its ability to side-step to adjacent protofilaments when it encounters obstacles on an MT.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of improvement in kinesin motility on MT bridges where the entire surface is accessible.

claim: Multiple motors can transport cargo under conditions in which single motors are unable to walk along MTs.
source: We asked whether multiple motors can transport cargo under conditions in which single motors are unable to walk along MTs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing that multi-motor cargos move processively at obstacle densities that completely inhibit single motors.

claim: Beads incubated with a low concentration (50 nM) of kinesin motors showed processive motility on MTs decorated with 7 QDs µm−1.
source: When the beads were incubated with a low concentration (50 nM) of kinesin motors, we detected processive motility of beads, albeit with frequent pausing, on MTs decorated with 7 QDs µm−1 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Motility of beads with 50 nM kinesin was severely inhibited at 12 QDs µm−1.
source: However, motility of these beads was severely inhibited at 12 QDs µm−1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: When beads were incubated with a higher concentration (1.5 µM) of kinesin, their mobile fraction was unaffected by the decoration of MTs with 12 QDs µm−1.
source: Surprisingly, when beads were incubated with a higher concentration (1.5 µM) of kinesin, their mobile fraction was unaffected by the decoration of MTs with 12 QDs µm−1 (Figure 5B,C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Multiple DDBs transported beads to the minus-ends of MTs regardless of the surface density of QDs with no decrease in mobile fraction.
source: Similarly, multiple DDBs transported beads to the minus-ends of MTs regardless of the surface density of QDs with no decrease in mobile fraction (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: The velocity of dynein-driven beads decreased by 28% in the presence of 12 QD µm−1.
source: The analysis of the individual trajectories of dynein-driven beads showed that the velocity decreased by 28% in the presence 12 QD µm−1 (p=0.02, two-tailed t-test, Figure 5C), comparable to a 19% decrease of the velocity of single dyneins under the same conditions (p=0.05, two-tailed t-test, Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The velocity of kinesin-driven beads decreased by 25% when exposed to 12 QDs µm−1.
source: The velocity of kinesin-driven beads also decreased by 25% decrease when exposed to 12 QDs µm−1 (p=0.02, two-tailed t-test, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: For beads coated with 1.5 µM of kinesin, run length and mobile fraction were unaffected by 20 µg/mL antibody.
source: For beads coated with 1.5 µM of kinesin, run length and mobile fraction were unaffected by 20 µg/mL antibody (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: All beads coated with 1.5 µM kinesin walked until they reached the end of the MT in the presence of 20 µg/mL antibody.
source: Remarkably, all beads walked until they reached the end of the MT (Figure 5D, Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Video 6.

claim: Multi-motor kinesin exhibited reduced velocity at 20 µg/mL antibody.
source: Similar to QD-obstacles, multi-motor kinesin exhibited reduced velocity at 20 µg/mL antibody (p=0.04, Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A team of kinesins can carry cargo beads over long distances along MTs densely decorated with obstacles as well as dyneins.
source: Therefore, while single kinesins are strongly affected by obstacles on MTs, a team of kinesins can carry cargo beads over long distances along MTs densely decorated with obstacles as well as dyneins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing comparable performance of multi-kinesin and multi-dynein cargos.

claim: Most beads driven by multiple kinesins or dyneins rotated to the top of the MT with no forward motion before they continued along the MTs when challenged by a PDMS wall.
source: Remarkably, we observed that most of these beads rotated to the top of the MT with no forward motion before they continued along the MTs (77 ± 13% kinesin beads and 85 ± 5% dynein beads, mean ± SD, Figure 6B,C, Videos 7 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C and Videos 7 and 8.

claim: 29% and 24% of kinesin- and dynein-driven beads, respectively, paused before moving forward when encountering a PDMS wall.
source: 29% and 24% of kinesin- and dynein-driven beads, respectively, paused before moving forward (Figure 6B,C), similar to intracellular cargos that encounter stationary organelles (Che et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Beads driven by multiple kinesins paused for a shorter period than dynein-driven beads when they encountered the wall (3.8 ± 0.2 s vs 7.8 ± 1.0 s, mean ± SEM).
source: In contrast to strong inhibition of single kinesins by obstacles, beads driven by multiple kinesins paused for a shorter period than dynein-driven beads when they encountered the wall (3.8 ± 0.2 s vs 7.8 ± 1.0 s, mean ± SEM, Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Only 23% of kinesin beads and 15% of dynein beads either got stuck or detached from MTs at the PDMS wall.
source: Only 23% of kinesin beads and 15% of dynein beads either got stuck or detached from MTs at the PDMS wall.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Cargos driven by multiple motors can bypass large obstacles by rotating around the circumference of the MT.
source: We concluded that cargos driven by multiple motors can bypass large obstacles by rotating around the circumference of the MT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing rotation of beads around MTs.

claim: Kinesin and dynein utilize different mechanisms to bypass obstacles.
source: These results show that kinesin and dynein utilize different mechanisms to bypass these obstacles.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations showing different responses of single kinesin and dynein to obstacles.

claim: Single dyneins were highly capable of maneuvering around obstacles on the MT.
source: Despite their large size, single dyneins were highly capable of maneuvering around obstacles on the MT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing high motility of single dyneins even at high obstacle densities.

claim: Single kinesins were strongly inhibited by obstacles.
source: In contrast, single kinesins were strongly inhibited by obstacles, as previously reported (Dixit et al., 2008; Leduc et al., 2012; Telley et al., 2009; Schneider et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the current study and prior research as indicated by the citations.

claim: The differences in obstacle avoidance between kinesin and dynein are likely a consequence of differences in the sidestepping ability of the two motors.
source: These results are likely a consequence of differences in the sidestepping ability of the two motors (Can et al., 2014; DeWitt et al., 2012; Ray et al., 1993).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and prior knowledge about motor stepping behavior.

claim: Multiple kinesins were able to bypass obstacles as efficiently as dyneins.
source: Remarkably, multiple kinesins were able to bypass these obstacles as efficiently as dyneins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing comparable performance of multi-kinesin and multi-dynein cargos.

claim: In the case of multi-motor cargos, kinesin motors are just as likely to get stuck at an obstacle as a single motor.
source: In the case of multi-motor cargos, we anticipate that kinesin motors are just as likely to get stuck at an obstacle as a single motor.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the properties of individual kinesin motors.

claim: The other motors driving the cargo may exert a force on the stuck motor, causing its rapid detachment and the continued forward motion of the cargo.
source: However, the other motors driving the cargo may exert a force on the stuck motor, causing its rapid detachment and the continued forward motion of the cargo (Tjioe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the mechanism of obstacle avoidance by multi-motor cargos, supported by citation.

claim: In the process of bypassing obstacles, new motors in the leading direction are recruited to the lattice while the motors in the trailing direction detach from the MT.
source: In this process, new motors in the leading direction are recruited to the lattice while the motors in the trailing direction detach from the MT.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the mechanism of obstacle avoidance by multi-motor cargos.

claim: A team of motors carrying the cargo pause until they move sideways either by stepping to neighboring protofilaments or because stochastic shifts in the center of mass of the bead allow for unbound motors to attach to adjacent protofilaments.
source: Alternatively, a team of motors carrying the cargo pause until they move sideways either by stepping to neighboring protofilaments or because stochastic shifts in the center of mass of the bead allow for unbound motors to attach to adjacent protofilaments.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis about the mechanism of obstacle avoidance by multi-motor cargos.

claim: Multi-motor teamwork proved beneficial for both types of motors when challenged by a large obstacle.
source: Multi-motor teamwork also proved beneficial for both types of motors when challenged by a large obstacle.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing that multi-motor cargos can bypass large PDMS walls.

claim: Cargo beads driven by multiple kinesin or dynein motors were able to maneuver around a PDMS obstruction that blocked access to half of the MT surface.
source: Cargo beads driven by multiple kinesin or dynein motors were able to maneuver around a PDMS obstruction that blocked access to half of the MT surface (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Correlative live-cell and super-resolution microscopy showed that rotational movement could be used by cargos to avoid steric obstacles.
source: In addition, correlative live-cell and super-resolution microscopy showed that rotational movement could be used by cargos to avoid steric obstacles (Verdeny-Vilanova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: Tug-of-war between opposite polarity motors is not required to bypass large obstacles.
source: While transient back-and-forth movement of cargo may allow it to change the protofilament track, our results clearly show that tug-of-war between opposite polarity motors is not required to bypass large obstacles.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that cargos driven by only one type of motor can bypass large obstacles.

claim: Fluidity of the cargo is not essential for bypassing large obstacles.
source: We also showed that fluidity of the cargo is not essential for this process (Verdeny-Vilanova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using rigid beads and contrasts with a prior hypothesis.

claim: Multiplicity of motors not only increases the collective force generation and the length of processive runs on an MT but also enables motors to maneuver around obstacles in their path.
source: These results show that multiplicity of motors not only increases the collective force generation and the length of processive runs on an MT but also enables motors to maneuver around obstacles in their path.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing improved obstacle avoidance by multi-motor cargos.

claim: Kinesin moves towards the plus-ends of MTs.
source: Kinesin and dynein move towards the plus- and minus-ends of MTs, respectively, and play major roles in intracellular cargo transport, cell locomotion, and division (Reck-Peterson et al., 2018; Verhey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about kinesin directionality supported by citations.

claim: Dynein moves towards the minus-ends of MTs.
source: Kinesin and dynein move towards the plus- and minus-ends of MTs, respectively, and play major roles in intracellular cargo transport, cell locomotion, and division (Reck-Peterson et al., 2018; Verhey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about dynein directionality supported by citations.

claim: Kinesin and dynein play major roles in intracellular cargo transport, cell locomotion, and division.
source: Kinesin and dynein move towards the plus- and minus-ends of MTs, respectively, and play major roles in intracellular cargo transport, cell locomotion, and division (Reck-Peterson et al., 2018; Verhey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: QDs are 25 nm in diameter.
source: To this end, we decorated biotinylated MTs with streptavidin-conjugated QDs (25 nm in diameter) (DeWitt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a specification of the QDs used in the study.

claim: Antibodies are small in size (~150 kDa).
source: Because antibodies are small in size (~150 kDa), they likely block fewer protofilaments than QD obstacles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about antibody size.

claim: Antibodies likely block fewer protofilaments than QD obstacles.
source: Because antibodies are small in size (~150 kDa), they likely block fewer protofilaments than QD obstacles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the size difference between antibodies and QDs.

claim: The maximum decoration of QD obstacles was 12 QDs µm−1.
source: The surface density of QD obstacles was varied, with a maximum decoration of 12 QDs µm−1 (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: On surface-immobilized MTs, motors cannot access protofilaments facing the coverslip.
source: On surface-immobilized MTs, motors cannot access protofilaments facing the coverslip.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the experimental setup.

claim: Surface immobilization may serve as an additional obstacle as the motors attempt to bypass the QDs.
source: As a result, surface immobilization may serve as an additional obstacle as the motors attempt to bypass the QDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the limitation of surface immobilization.

claim: MTs in the cell are freely suspended in 3D.
source: MTs in the cell, however, are freely suspended in 3D.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the cellular environment.

claim: Freely suspended MTs may allow motors to fully explore the MT surface and more successfully bypass the obstacles.
source: This may allow motors to fully explore the MT surface and more successfully bypass the obstacles.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is tested using MT bridges.

claim: In cells, cargos are often carried by multiple motors.
source: In cells, cargos are often carried by multiple motors, which increases collective force generation and enables transport of the cargo over longer distances (Derr et al., 2012; Rai et al., 2016; Encalada et al., 2011; Levi et al., 2006) as well as at slightly higher velocities (Nelson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Multiple motors increase collective force generation.
source: In cells, cargos are often carried by multiple motors, which increases collective force generation and enables transport of the cargo over longer distances (Derr et al., 2012; Rai et al., 2016; Encalada et al., 2011; Levi et al., 2006) as well as at slightly higher velocities (Nelson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Multiple motors enable transport of the cargo over longer distances.
source: In cells, cargos are often carried by multiple motors, which increases collective force generation and enables transport of the cargo over longer distances (Derr et al., 2012; Rai et al., 2016; Encalada et al., 2011; Levi et al., 2006) as well as at slightly higher velocities (Nelson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In vivo studies have observed both anterograde and retrograde cargos to bypass stationary organelles.
source: In vivo studies have observed both anterograde and retrograde cargos to bypass stationary organelles (Che et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by prior research as indicated by the citation.

claim: It has been proposed that rotation of cargoes around the MT requires the presence of both kinesin and dynein motors on the cargo or the distortion of the lipid cargo.
source: It has been proposed that rotation of cargoes around the MT requires the presence of both kinesin and dynein motors on the cargo or the distortion of the lipid cargo (Hancock, 2014; Kaplan et al., 2018; Verdeny-Vilanova et al., 2017).
